trans.sense: a large drum played with the hands

examples.text: There are three principal types of traditional drums in Guinean Sousou culture: the djembe, the dundun, and the tama. The djembe is a single-headed goblet-shaped drum with a relatively high-pitched tone.
examples.ref: 2007, Karin Gaynell Patterson, Expressions of Africa in Los Angeles Public Performance, 1781—1994, page 133:

examples.text: The djembe is one of the best-known and popular African drums, particular with those in the West who are interested in learning a drumming tradition.
examples.ref: 2009, Tamara Dean, Composition for Computer Musicians, page 51:

examples.text: The djembe has become the most recognizable drum from West Africa, with a history that can be traced to the twelfth century Mali Empire and the Mandinka people.
examples.ref: 2010, Randy Raine-Reusch, Play the World: The 101 World Instrument Primer, page 91:

examples.text: Very few djembes are perfectly round. Most are slightly egg- or triangle-shaped. Lack of roundness is not a problem for sound: many such djembes sound excellent.
